triples.relationship: Animal imagery: a bear in a scene of violent destruction
triples.rationale: Daniel sees a bear-like beast with ribs in its mouth commanded to devour much flesh; the interpretation later calls the beasts kingdoms. Hosea portrays God meeting Israel like a distressed bear and tearing the heart's enclosure, followed by devouring lion cubs and tearing beasts. Both employ a bear amid bodily destruction, but Hosea's divine comparison is not identified with Daniel's kingdom. Hosea does not explain the three ribs or one-sided stance, and its bear is in distress rather than expressly bereaved.
triples.source_text: After her there was another beast with the likeness of a bear. It stood on one side and had three ribs in its mouth. He spoke in this way: ‘Rise, devour much flesh!’

target_units.text: I will meet them like a bear in distress and tear open their heart’s enclosure. There forest lion cubs will devour them; field beasts will tear them apart.

triples.relationship: Royal imagery: Egypt's power represented by a disabled arm
triples.rationale: Daniel says Egypt's king will not prevail because his arm cannot establish strength and his arm and his companions' arms grow numb. Ezekiel portrays Pharaoh's arms as shattered and unhealed, unable to gain strength to hold a sword. Both express the failure of Egyptian royal power through disabled arms. Numbness and fracture remain different images, and no personal identity or shared campaign is claimed for the unnamed kings or Daniel's treaty journey.
triples.source_text: At the completion of years he will lead them, and the king of Egypt will enter the northern kingdom to make treaties. He will not prevail, for his arm will not establish strength; his arm and that of those traveling with him will grow numb, and he will remain until the appointed hours.

target_units.text: “Son of man, I shattered the arms of Pharaoh king of Egypt. Behold, it has not been bound up to provide healing, to put a poultice upon it, to give strength to grasp a sword.

triples.relationship: Narrative comparison: a report redirects an invading ruler
triples.rationale: Daniel describes a report from the east and north disturbing the ruler and prompting an angry, destructive departure. Isaiah's word in Kings says the Assyrian ruler will hear a report and return to his land; the narrative then reports news of an Ethiopian king coming to fight him. In both, incoming news changes the course of a hostile ruler's activity. The directions and report are not identified as the same, and Daniel's renewed killing differs from the promised return and eventual death in Kings.
triples.source_text: A report from the east and north will disturb him, and he will go out in strong anger and with a sword to wipe out and kill many.

target_units.text: Isaiah said to them, ‘Tell your master: Thus says the Lord: Do not fear the words you have heard, with which the king of the Assyrians’ young servants blasphemed.
Behold, I am putting a spirit within him. He shall hear a report and return to his land, and I shall bring him down by the sword in his land.’
Rhapsakes returned and found the king of the Assyrians fighting against Lomna, for he had heard that he had departed from Lachish.
